easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count. The
  clock isn't a budget or a target.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

## 9. The tubes here

The historical names in this note correspond to these tubes: ochers and
yellow earths → yellow ochre; red earths and red iron oxide → red earth;
cinnabar → vermilion; the green pigments → green earth, copper green and
Rinmann's green.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with ground layers laid from the tubes.
- **Paint.** Pigment from the tubes with an oil-medium share.
- **Taking paint off.** A brush picks up wet paint as it passes; that is
  how paint comes off the canvas.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and stout branches, the upper level ascending and the lower drooping". Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load.
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce"). Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes.
- **Bark.** Orange-brown. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches.

### 3.8 Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*)

- **Habit.** 23–27 m on average, sometimes over 40 m. It lives 400 years or more. Crowns are rounded when young and round-topped when old. The trunk is often twisted, depending on seed origin. In some conifers, flattening and broadening of the crown may be the only sign of old-age retrenchment.
- **Bark.** The upper stem is "a distinct reddish-orange," while the lower part is "furrowed brown to grey-brown and becomes deeply fissured". "Upper crowns always show orange peeling bark".
- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted.

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

-- The trees.  Each is an upright axis; heavy limbs leave near the top of the shoots,
-- sweep out at 50-80 degrees, then turn up; secondaries leave those in turn.
-- Only three orders are drawn: the finest twigs are left to the paint.
gA, gB, gC = pencil("4B"), pencil("B"), pencil("H")

local function curve(x, y, ang, len, bend, n)
  local pts, a, px, py = {{x, y}}, ang, x, y
  for i = 1, n do
    a = a + bend / n + randn(0, 0.03)
    px, py = px + math.cos(a) * len / n, py + math.sin(a) * len / n
    pts[#pts + 1] = {px, py}
  end
  return pts, px, py, a
end

local function limb(x, y, ang, len, order, grav)
  local bend = -grav * rand(0.5, 1.0)          -- grav>0 turns the tip upward
  local pts, tx, ty, ta = curve(x, y, ang, len, bend, 4)
  local g, pr = gA, 0.8
  if order == 2 then g, pr = gB, 0.6 else g, pr = gC, 0.45 end
  g:line(pts, {pressure=pr, smooth=true})
  if order >= 3 then return end
  local n = (order == 0) and 3 or 2
  for i = 1, n do
    if rand() < 0.8 then
      local t = i / (n + 1)
      local j = 1 + math.floor(t * 3)
      local bx, by = pts[j][1], pts[j][2]
      local s = (i % 2 == 0) and -1 or 1
      limb(bx, by, ta + s * rand(0.6, 1.1), len * rand(0.38, 0.58), order + 1, grav + 0.25)
    end
  end
  return tx, ty, ta
end

maskOf = function(list, first, last)
  local m
  for k = first, last do
    local b = list[k]
    local n, ws = #b.pts, {}
    for i = 1, n do
      local t = (i - 1) / (n - 1)
      ws[i] = b.w0 + (b.w1 - b.w0) * t
    end
    local r = ribbon(b.pts, ws)
    m = (m == nil) and r or (m + r)

Done, day 51. The picture: a lake among hills at dusk, the sun gone down behind the far peak; a woman with a bundle of faggots stands at the water's edge with her boat, not going in yet; two bare oaks cropped by the frame, fog on the water, birds gone home.

What the easel taught me this time, all of it the hard way:
- `work`'s coverage takes a number, not a function; a graded mask is what varies density. `stipple`'s coverage does take a function.
- A cover paint only covers if something in the pile hides. Umber, smalt, pale smalt and green earth are stains; lead white and bone black are the body. Everything I wanted dark had to be built on bone black.
- `fill=true` is what completes a passage. Without it, high coverage still leaves the underlayer showing.
- The softest masks are the ones that misbehave: with a low threshold and fill, a veil I meant for the feet of a range painted the whole lake white. Mask the veil to its own region.
- Paint from the tubes, with little or no medium, reads as colour. Piles thinned with oil came out warm, whatever the pigment, because the warm ground comes through.
- A global glaze with long low-pressure strokes leaves the loaded start of every stroke behind as an opaque lozenge. One of those cost me the whole picture; I rebuilt it region by region.
- Over a wet film, a light pass lifts and smears what is under it. Wait for dry, and lay the incident last.
- Oil-rich lead-white glazes stay tacky for five weeks. That is why a blob of one took a month to cover.

Where it falls short of what I aimed at: the trees are sticks rather than oaks, and the lake is soft where it should be glassy.

**The Ninth Hour**

A lake among the hills at dusk, the sun just gone down behind the far peak, so the last of the light lies in a warm band along the horizon and the ranges above it have gone to cold grey. Fog sits on the water and eats the feet of the hills; the dark near range at the left and the pale peak at the right are the only two planes, and the lake repeats them, broken by ripples. Two bare oaks, cropped by the top and bottom of the picture, stand on the near bank; at the water's edge a woman with a bundle of faggots on her shoulder waits beside her drawn-up boat, small and dark against the light, and the birds have already gone over.

It is painted in Friedrich's manner as far as the easel allowed: warm ground under lead white, a graphite underdrawing, thin films from the tubes rather than blended passages, gradations by stipple and by paint pooling, few pigments. Where it falls short of the aim: the trees read more as poles than oaks, and the lake is soft where it should be glassy — one careless glaze cost me the whole surface early on, and I rebuilt it region by region.

# Paint a picture

Compose and paint one original landscape in the manner of Caspar David

- The folder [local path redacted] this brief, your notes and the easel.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in

events.text:
Now the lake is a flat dark grey-brown slab. Too dark, too warm-brown, too even. It reads like a mudflat, and the horizon is a hard straight line. This is a blank canvas for the water — which is fine as a base, but now I have to build the whole lake: gradient, reflection, light.

Problems:
1. The colour is too warm/olive-brown. It needs to be cool blue-grey. Raw umber 2.6 is dominating. Let me use a cooler pile: more smalt/pale smalt, less umber, and a touch of Prussian blue? Prussian blue has tinting strength 3.0 — powerful but useful for cooling. Friedrich's darks are cool.
2. The value is now nearly uniform; needs a gradient: lighter at the far end (reflecting the misty sky), darker near the shore.
3. The horizon line is hard and dead straight — because I laid a full-width horizontal cover to y=450 while the far shore/mist is around 440-455. Actually the mist band got covered too (the mist used to lie at y 430-455). Look: the mist strip above the water is now a thin bright band at y≈445-455 and the far shore line is razor sharp. Hmm, actually the far bank/mist is still there above y=450. The hard line at y≈452 is my cover's top edge — the cover stopped exactly at 450 with a 9-unit ramp. Because the mist band above is pale and the lake below is now dark, there's a hard value edge.

I need to fix that: the water's edge at the far shore should be lost in mist. So: a band of mist/fog straddling y 440-470, painted with a pale veil that softens the join. And the far shore line itself should not be perfectly straight — it should be broken, with the mist lying in.

So plan for the lake now, in order:
 (a) Cool and lighten the lake a touch: a cool glaze (pale smalt + smalt + a little Prussian blue, tiny umber) at low coverage, then a value gradient.
 (b) Gradient: near the far shore a pale cool veil (mist reflected), deepening toward the viewer.
 (c) The mirror: under the far shore, the reflection of the ranges — soft dark horizontal bands; under the big peak, a pale column.
 (d) Broken light: crisp horizontal strokes.
 (e) Near the bank: darker, with a few long drags.

That's a lot of passes, each needing dry time. Alternatively I can build the gradient directly into the cover by using `coverage=function(x,y)` (stipple takes a function for coverage; work's coverage takes a number per my lesson — "work's coverage takes a number, not a function; a graded mask is what varies density"). So to vary density I use masks. OK: I'll glaze with graded masks.

Step (a)+(b) can be one chunk if the glaze piles are thin and I use graded masks — but successive glazes in the same chunk over wet-under would lift. Each glaze over wet paint = smearing. However, glazing the same colour over itself while it goes off... risky.

Let me be smart: paint one glaze per chunk, and use `wait` between chunks only as needed (the paint operations themselves take time; a long pass takes an hour+, and lead-white-free glazes dry in a day). I'll check drying between steps.

Now, colour target: the lake should read as a cool blue-grey, in shadow, so it goes slightly green-blue or blue-violet against the warm sky. Right now it's brown-grey. Let me mix: pale smalt 2.6, smalt 2.2, lead white 1, raw umber 1.2, Prussian blue 0.35. Prussian blue's tinting 3.0 → 0.35 parts is a meaningful amount. Let me test on a small patch first? Better: paint the whole lake and look; if too blue, glaze back.

Hmm — careful about "a stain is not a covering": pale smalt + smalt are stains (hiding 0.3-0.35), so a glaze of them won't hide much; it will tint. That's what I want for a glaze: it shifts the hue toward blue-grey. Combined with the dark glaze underneath, it should cool it.

Let me do it: cool glaze with coverage ~2, fill, horizontal.

Actually, better idea for both cooling AND grading in one pass: use `coverage` via a graded mask. I'll do:
 - mCool = mOpen (full) with cool glaze at coverage 2.2.
Then next chunk:
 - gradient darkening with waterDarkP over mGradDeep (mask increasing with y).

Let me go. And to save time, I'll combine the cool glaze and the far mist-veil into one chunk? Different piles = different passes in the same chunk over wet-under. The veil is at the top and the cool glaze covers the whole lake including the top... Overlap would smear. Let me keep the cool glaze to y > 462 and let the mist veil handle 440-470 later (drawn on top, after dry).

wait

Far too blue — Prussian blue at 0.4 parts with tinting 3.0 is way too strong, and it deposited as blobs (the glaze hand leaves loaded lozenges — the lesson about "A global glaze with long low-pressure strokes leaves the loaded start of every stroke behind as an opaque lozenge"). 1. Reduce Prussian blue drastically (0.4 → 0.06) or drop it and rely on smalt. The problem is that a glaze deposits unevenly (blobs). I need less coverage, more even, and no super-tinting pigment.

**The light on the lake**

Sources of light on the water:
(a) The far shore mist band: pale, soft, straddling the water's edge (y 440-475). Also the mist sits ON the water for a bit.
(b) The reflection of the pale far peak: a vertical column of soft light from x≈560-900, strongest just below the shore, broken by ripples into horizontal dashes, fading downward to about y 540.
(c) The reflection of the warm glow (the orange band at x 550-950, y 230-330 in the sky): on the water it would be a warm sheen in the same x range, low intensity, around y 480-580.

(e) The near water (y 600-660) is dark; a few long pale dashes where the sky is bright? Friedrich keeps the near water dark with a few glints.
(f) Ripple structure: horizontal dashes everywhere, denser near the horizon, sparser and longer near the viewer (perspective!). That's an important truth of water: near the far shore ripples are compressed (short dashes), near the viewer they're long and sparse. I should encode that: short dashes at y 460-520, medium at 520-600, long and few at 600-660.

I'll draw these with a rigger brush loaded with a light pile (lead white + yellow ochre + a little pale smalt), making individual horizontal strokes with slight thickness variation and rounded ends, clustered in bands with gaps.

events.text:
day 180, finished: "Evening on the Upland Lake".

The picture: an upland lake after sundown. The sun has gone down behind the hill on the right; its last light is a warm band low in the sky and on the flank of the pale peak. Mist lies on the water at the far shore and a low wooded bank shows through it. The lake is dark and quiet — the peak is in it upside down as a pale wedge, and a few long drags are all the movement there is. Two bare trees, cropped by the left edge, stand on the near bank; their fine branchlets are the most delicate thing in the picture. At the water's edge a woman stands with her bundle of faggots on her shoulder and her boat drawn up beside her, not going in yet. Birds are going home. Mood: waiting.

What this last stretch taught me, all of it expensively:
- rect(x, y, w, h) takes a HEIGHT. I passed the second y for a week of painting time; every "band" ran to the bottom edge and buried the trees, the bank, the figure. Build bands from mask(function(x,y)) instead — it cannot get this wrong.
- A light glaze over dark, wet paint lifts it. And a bright pile with fill=true scatters flat pale lozenges that read as leaves or scum. Mist is a low-contrast veil at low pressure, nothing else.
- Reflections on water are carried by tone, not by marks. Every attempt to draw the light — dashes, drags, stipple — read as sparks or scribble. What works: darken the lake, then lift a soft wedge under the mountain and blend it.
- stipple's coverage does take a function(x, y), and that is the only honest way to get a gradient: `work`'s coverage is a single number and a soft mask only softens the edge, it does not thin the paint. But stipple leaves specks — do not use it where the surface must stay smooth.
- A trunk's pale core came back twice: it was not enough coverage, not a wrong colour. Bone black at coverage 4 with fill finally held.
- The trees are better and still not oaks. The fine branchlets changed them from a diagram into a tree; what they cannot do is untaper a limb that was drawn as a bar.

Where it falls short: the limbs are still bars at 1:1, the bank is a smooth mound, and the far shore's line is straighter than I would choose.

**Evening on the Upland Lake**

An upland lake after sundown. The sun has gone down behind the hill on the right; its last light is a warm band low in the sky and along the flank of the pale peak, while mist lies on the water at the far shore with a low wooded bank showing through it. The lake is dark and quiet — the mountain sits in it upside down as a soft pale wedge, and a few long drags are all the movement there is. Two bare trees, cropped by the left edge, stand on the near bank, their fine branchlets the most delicate thing in the picture; at the water's edge a woman stands with her bundle of faggots on her shoulder and her boat drawn up beside her, not going in yet. Birds are going home. The mood is waiting.

Coming back to it, the lake and the trees were the two weaknesses I had noted, and both took far longer than they should have. The lake ended up rebuilt from scratch — a calm dark surface with the reflection carried by tone rather than by drawn ripples — and the trees were given some thousands of fine branchlets, which turned a diagram of sticks into trees, though the limbs are still visibly bars at arm's length. I also destroyed a good deal of the picture along the way by misreading `rect` as taking corners rather than a width and height, which ran several veils and mist bands off the bottom of the canvas and buried the trees, the bank and the figure until I rebuilt them.

Actually — think harder about whether this will improve the painting. Friedrich's bare trees: the trunks are usually dark silhouettes against sky, with a subtle light on one side. The risk: painting a light strip on a dark trunk could look like a painted stripe if too uniform. Use a graded coverage function (via stipple coverage function, or work with a mask that fades) and low pressure, plus some breaks.

Better approach: build the lit side as a mask = trunk mask × (a horizontal falloff toward the right edge). But "don't encode an image in masks" — I think the intent of that rule is to forbid encoding a whole picture (e.g. drawing an image by setting mask values from pixel data). Building a gradient mask as a light model is a normal painterly operation (I did that with mLight etc. in earlier chunks — chunk 184 `softdash`, chunk 220 `mRidgeV` etc. which used function masks).

Hmm, but there's a subtlety: the rule about "Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates." Using the trunk mask itself (a drawn shape, saved in a global) and taking its rim on one side is not mirroring — it's derived from the same drawn shape. That's like painting with the brush along one side. I think it's acceptable: it's "painting the light with a mask of the form", which is standard practice.

events.text:
day 212: back to the picture after the bank, day 199. I had left it "finished"; the bank was the one passage I had always known was weak — a smooth olive mound with nothing in it — and the trunks were flat bars.

What I did, and what each thing cost:

- The trunks. Three attempts at giving them a lit flank: a pale zipper down each one, then a chain of beads where I covered it, then a rim light set in from the edge that read as strips of tape. All three were the same error: I mixed a "slightly lighter than the trunk" pile and it came out three times too light, because a trunk that reads black on the canvas is a pile with a great deal of bone black in it and any white or ochre at all changes it. They are silhouettes against a sunset sky, and silhouettes want nothing done to them. I gave them a few dark bark knots instead and left them.
- The bank. Four passes and two reversals. First it came out bright olive, then, when I put white into a "ridge" pile, as a strip of butter; then I made it the darkest mass in the picture, which was right, and it is what it is now — a dark mottled ground with a fringe of grass along its edge and nothing in the middle. Every attempt at light incident on it (yellow tussocks, pale stones, a bleached stick, a dry scumble) came out as sparks, eyes, chalk scratches or a flat haze, and each one had to be scrubbed back. The rule I ended on: a dark mass wants its interest at its edge, not in its middle.
- The cast shadows I put on the bank lifted the still-open paint and left pale ghosts of the ground; the warm glaze I tried later laid visible stripes and lifted again in the one place the bank was still open. A glaze is not a repair.

Where the picture now falls short, honestly: the bank is empty, the limbs are still bars, and the far shore's line is straighter than I would choose. I would rather stop here than keep correcting — every further stroke I have put into those three things this month has made them worse, and the easel is not the place to argue with a decision I have now made three times.

I stopped there.

**"Evening on the Upland Lake"**

An upland lake after sundown: the sun has gone down behind the hill on the right, and its last light is a warm band low in the sky and along the flank of the pale peak. Mist lies on the water at the far shore, where a low reed bed shows through it. The lake is dark and glassy — the peak is in it upside down as a pale wedge, and a handful of long drags are all the movement there is. Two bare oaks, cropped by the left edge, stand in silhouette on the near bank, their fine branchlets the most delicate thing in the picture. At the water's edge a woman waits with her bundle of faggots on her shoulder and her boat drawn up beside her; the birds are going home.

This last stretch went into the two passages I knew were weakest. The trunks are now even silhouettes with a little bark in them — three attempts at modelling a lit flank on them all came out too light, and I stopped. The near bank, which had been a smooth olive mound the same value as the water, is now the darkest mass in the picture, quiet and mottled, with its interest at the edge in the fringe of grass. The boat's rim was knocked back so it stops shouting. It is not a finished-masterpiece landscape: the bank is empty, the limbs are still bars, and the far shore's line is straighter than I would choose.

day 224, 16:40: Back to the far shore — the one passage my last note called too straight. What I did and what it cost:

- GOOD: I laid five bare trees rising above the shore line, with a second small tree and two more at uneven intervals, each stem hand-plotted and stroked with a rigger at falling pressure so it tapers. Lozenges are not a mistake of colour or coverage, they are a mistake of stroke size against shape size. Small strokes (hand="detail", 4-14 units) over the same masks gave a fine broken tone instead. - The cover works and costs four days each time: a light veil of mistFix at coverage 3, fill, over the blots, after the blots are dry, buries them and matches the surrounding mist almost exactly. I have now done this twice.

events.name: note
events.text:
day 228, 17:00: Done this time, and I mean it.

The reflection under the far shore is in, and it is the third way I have tried it. The first two (a dark smear, then a band of grey) both came out as evenly spaced lozenges and had to be covered; what worked was hand="detail" over short, blurred ellipse segments — small strokes, 5-14 units, against a band 6-8 units thick — which broke the reflection into a fine mottled grain, and then ONE set of long horizontal smear passes with a clean soft brush while it was still wet, which turned the row of separate marks into one continuous band with a rippled lower edge. Small marks first, then merge them wet: that is the recipe for a reflection, and it is the same recipe I use for water anywhere.

Standing back: the middle distance is now a low broken line of wood along the far waterline, seven bare trees standing out of it at uneven intervals, mist over its base, mist swallowing its right-hand end, and the wood's own dark grain reflected in the mist just below. Before this week that passage was a comb. It is the part of the picture I am proudest of.

Also settled, after looking hard at it for a while and nearly repainting it: the pale broken streak at y 628-640 on the right is not scum floating on the lake, it is the lit crest of the near bank rising to the right, with the scrub on it. I was wrong twice about what it was before I measured it against a grid and found the bank mass immediately below it. Measure before you decide that a passage is wrong.

Where the picture still falls short, and I am leaving it there: the limbs of the near trees are still bars at 1:1, and the bank is still empty in the middle. Both have been corrected three times this month and both got worse. The sky's cloud grain is regular if you stand close to it, and that I chose to leave rather than glaze over a sky that works.

**"Evening on the Upland Lake"** (72 × 56 cm, oil on linen)

This session I went back to the one passage my last notes called weak — the far shore — and rebuilt it. The line of reeds that had been a comb is now a low broken band of wood along the far waterline, clumped and gapped, with seven bare trees standing out of it at uneven intervals; mist swallows its base and its right-hand end. Under it, in the water, is the shore's own dark grain reflected as a soft continuous band.

What it cost: two lozenge disasters that each took four days of drying and a full cover with mist paint before I could repair them. The lesson is mechanical and I have written it down — a "body" stroke is 20–60 units long, and when my masks were 90 units wide and 12 tall, one stroke covered the whole shape and its outline became the mark. Small strokes over small shapes, then merged while wet with a clean soft brush, is what actually builds a reflection.

I also spent time nearly repainting a pale streak on the right that I took for scum on the lake; measured against a grid it turned out to be the lit crest of the near bank, and I left it alone.

Left standing: the near trees' limbs are still bars at arm's length, and the bank is still empty through the middle. Both have been corrected three times now and both got worse each time.
